A1.justification: Despite the changed title and substantial expansion, both PDFs describe the same mechanistic study of DPO and toxicity. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices—A–E in v2 and A–K in v3—are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original GPT-2 Medium activation-patching and ablation experiments, toxicity measurements, and neuron-level projection analyses, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 reports original patching and activation-editing experiments across four models, probe validation, correlation analyses, and toxic-subspace investigations.

M1.justification: v2 intervenes by copying mean post-DPO activations into the pretrained model. v3 Section 6 adds independent activation editing: select a fraction of neurons and multiplicatively adjust activations according to their alignment and activation sign. It provides both learned-probe and token-embedding representations, eliminating dependence on post-DPO activations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the RealToxicityPrompts challenge subset, Jigsaw toxicity classification data, WikiText-2-derived preference pairs, and WikiText/Wikipedia language-quality evaluation. The evaluated tasks and data coverage remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and editing procedures do not introduce new datasets or task domains.

E2.justification: The untreated model and DPO remain comparators. v3 adds directly evaluated probe steering in Tables 2 and 12; v2 only discusses its effectiveness through earlier work. Conversely, v2 Table 1's zero-ablation and positive-only toxic-neuron intervention comparators are absent from v3.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B, and Mistral-7B configurations, replaces Perspective API toxicity scoring with Detoxify, and reports log perplexity instead of perplexity. Toxic-neuron tests change from 128 neurons to 256 plus a toxic-token subset identified using GPT-4o. New editing experiments vary intervention strength, neuron fraction, and selection strategy.

E4.justification: Beyond retained group-patching and neuron-rank analyses, v3 adds steering/editing sensitivity tests, alternative neuron-selection comparisons, patching of toxicity-increasing neurons, activation-shift correlations, and a three-direction toxic-subspace investigation (Appendices D and G–K). v2's zero-ablation and standalone TN/AN group tests are removed. These substantially expand the mechanisms and failure conditions investigated.

E5.justification: v3 Table 17 introduces Pearson correlation tests with p-values, absent from v2. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals for intervention performance. Figure 4's standard deviations describe variation across neurons, not uncertainty across repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for three additional models and both editing methods. GPT-2 untreated/DPO/four-group toxicity scores change from 0.453/0.208/0.114 in v2 Table 1 to 0.545/0.210/0.139 in v3 Table 2, under a different toxicity evaluator, so these are not same-setting performance changes. Exact Mistral comparisons are limited by conflicting DPO toxicity values in v3 Tables 2 and 19: 0.191 versus 0.221.

T1.justification: The original neuron-projection equation and four-group partition are retained under revised notation. v3 Appendix A extends the weighted-value-vector decomposition to gated MLPs, and Appendix G adds mathematical reasoning about projections onto an SVD-derived subspace. These are limited formal extensions, rather than a new theorem or proof framework.

C1.justification: v3 broadens the mechanistic claims from GPT-2 to four models and introduces a major practical contribution: activation editing claimed to outperform DPO without weight updates or post-DPO information. Its headline 2.5%–24% result concerns patched toxicity-score reduction; v2's 4.9% claim concerns dampened neurons' share of projection reduction, so these are different quantities.

C2.justification: Opposing neuron effects already appear in v2 Appendix D. v3 substantially extends their interpretation through regularisation and shallow-safety arguments, a regression-to-the-mean explanation for activation correlations, and explicit editing/F1 tradeoffs. It also qualifies late-layer effects as potentially probe-dependent and replaces a proposed future subspace analysis with documented difficulties assigning coherent groups.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents model specifications, greedy decoding, the 90:10 probe split, RMSprop training with learning rate 1e-5, training budgets, and model-specific regularisation weights (Tables 8–11). It also supplies editing parameters and contrastive token sets. These substantially improve implementation disclosure; they do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed. The code repository link is unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning beyond testing Lee et al.'s toxic-neuron explanation, connecting the work to activation steering, direct feature attribution, shallow alignment, and token-embedding geometry. Relevant additions include Panickssery et al., Zou et al., Makelov et al., Qi et al., and Lee et al. (2025). The earlier comparison to Suau et al.'s neural interventions disappears.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, setup, and discussion are substantially rewritten. v3 moves the MLP explanation into the main text, divides the former tracking analysis into separate sections, adds a distinct editing section, merges discussion and conclusion, and reorganises the appendices. The title, author list, and neuron-group terminology also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and redesigns the main results table around four models and intervention families. Existing group and layer plots are relocated and expanded, while opposing-effect panels, activation-distribution plots, and numerous technical and validation tables are added. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's single-model, post-DPO-dependent demonstration through four-model validation and independent activation editing. Sensitivity tests, the unsuccessful subspace investigation, and detailed training settings improve evidential depth and reproducibility. Editing still reduces F1, and conflicting Mistral values in Tables 2 and 19 require qualification of performance claims. These weaknesses limit precise conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in testing and documenting the proposed mechanism.
